title: Jensen Huang's $75 Million Gift to Vanderbilt Puts Art and Design at Heart of San Francisco Campus
excerpt: The Nvidia CEO and his wife's landmark matching donation will establish a new college of art, architecture and design on the site of the closing California College of the Arts.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • Jensen Huang and Lori pledged $75 million for a new art college at Vanderbilt's San Francisco campus.
  • The gift has spurred over $100 million in total investment, with 40% of the match already secured.
  • Vanderbilt's San Francisco campus will open in 2027, serving around 1,000 students.
  • Huang previously donated $22.5 million to rescue the California College of the Arts in 2025.

Vanderbilt University Announcement

A Tech Fortune Flows Into the Arts

Nvidia co-founder and CEO Jensen Huang is doubling down on his commitment to San Francisco's cultural ecosystem. On July 21, Vanderbilt University announced that a $75 million matching gift from Huang and his wife, Lori, will fund the creation of the Jen-Hsun and Lori Huang College of Art, Architecture and Design — the flagship academic unit of Vanderbilt's new San Francisco campus.

The college will anchor a campus that Vanderbilt plans to open in 2027 on the site of the closing California College of the Arts near Potrero Hill. A national search is underway for the inaugural dean.

"Technology expands what we can build. Art and design determine why we build it. Together they shape civilization."

— Jensen Huang, Nvidia CEO
> **"Together they shape civilization."

— Jensen Huang, Nvidia CEO

The matching gift has already attracted significant additional support."**

The matching gift has already attracted significant additional support. Total philanthropic commitments for the San Francisco campus have crossed $100 million, with over 40 percent of the match secured well ahead of the Dec. 31, 2028 deadline. Early donors include Vanderbilt alumni Katie and Matt Paige, Jeff and Marieke Rothschild, and Leah and Ben Spero.

From Rescue to Reinvention

The new college represents the latest chapter in a saga that began with CCA's financial crisis. The 120-year-old institution — San Francisco's last remaining private nonprofit art school — faced a $20 million deficit and declining enrollment that dropped from 1,848 students in 2019 to roughly 1,300 by 2024.

In February 2025, the Jen-Hsun and Lori Huang Foundation stepped in with a $22.5 million matching donation, the largest gift in CCA's history. More than 50 donors matched the amount, temporarily stabilizing the institution with $45 million in combined support. But the reprieve proved insufficient. In January 2026, CCA announced it would wind down operations by the end of the 2026-27 year, and Vanderbilt agreed to acquire the campus.

"San Francisco offers an extraordinary environment for learning across art, architecture, design and culture," Chancellor Daniel Diermeier said. "In partnership with the city and surrounding community, we will blend Vanderbilt's distinctive excellence with San Francisco's distinctive excellence to build something truly remarkable, together."

Huang Family Philanthropy Overview

The Vanderbilt gift is part of a broader philanthropic pattern from the Huang family. In November 2025, the Huangs committed a multi-year donation to the San Francisco Opera, funding the world premiere of The Monkey King, a new opera performed in English and Mandarin. The Jen-Hsun and Lori Huang Foundation — which holds more than $8 billion in Nvidia stock — has also donated $50 million to Oregon State University, $30 million to Stanford, and $108 million in computing resources for university researchers.

The scale of Huang's giving reflects the extraordinary wealth generated by Nvidia's dominance in AI chips. The foundation's minimum annual payout requirement now exceeds $700 million, given Nvidia's soaring valuation.

Bay Area's Indian Tech Community Watches Closely

For Indian professionals working at the intersection of technology and design in the Bay Area — one of the largest concentrations of Indian-origin tech workers globally — the new college signals an institutional commitment to interdisciplinary education where design thinking and creative practice are increasingly central. The Huang model of investing heavily in arts alongside technology offers a framework that positions creative practice not as a luxury but as a core component of innovation.

What's Next

Vanderbilt expects to welcome its first students to San Francisco in the 2027-28 academic year, pending regulatory approvals. The university will establish a CCA Institute to preserve the school's legacy through the Wattis Institute for Contemporary Arts, archival preservation, and alumni engagement for CCA's more than 25,000 graduates. With campuses now in Nashville, New York City, San Francisco, and soon West Palm Beach, Vanderbilt is executing one of the most ambitious geographic expansions in American higher education.
